articles.title: Calling All Builders: Meet Orca Security at AWS re:Invent 2026
articles.context: This is an invitation-only evening for technology, cloud, and security leaders, and space is limited
articles.full_text:
Software isn’t just built by developers anymore. Business teams, citizen developers, and AI agents are all shipping apps now, on top of more code, more models, and more cloud than ever. AWS re:Invent is where the people doing that building get together, and we can’t think of a better place to be.

We’re heading to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4 to talk about what it takes to move fast and still know what you’re shipping. For us, the answer is context: deep, accurate, actionable security that travels with your cloud and AI from development to runtime.

Here’s where to find the Orca Pod.

1. Visit us at Booth #886 at the Venetian Expo

Stop by to see how Orca shows you what your teams have actually built, including what’s coming out of AI app generation platforms, and connects the dots across code, cloud, identities, and AI workloads. Not just “this bucket is public,” but which change made it public and who owns it. That’s the difference between an alert and something your team can actually fix.

We’ll also have cold brew in the booth, Dec 1 to Dec 3, from 10am to 1pm, plus our prize wheel. Spin it, sip something cold, and stay as long as the questions keep coming.

And yes, there’s swag! Get a demo and take home an Orkie, plus socks, Rubik’s cubes, tumblers, and Orkie toys for the four-legged members of your team

Dates: November 30 to December 3Times: 4pm to 7pm Monday (Welcome Reception), 10am to 6pm Tuesday and Wednesday, 10am to 4pm ThursdayLocation: Booth #886, Venetian Expo

2. Meet 1:1 with Orca executives

The show floor isn’t always the best place for a real conversation. We’ve set aside private meeting rooms so you can sit down with Orca leadership and experts to talk through your cloud and AI security priorities.

Want to see how Orca gives builders and security teams the context to ship with confidence on AWS? Request a meeting and our team will reach out to find a date and time that works for you.

Dates: November 30 to December 3Times: By appointmentLocation: The Palazzo and The Venetian

3. Kick off the week at F1 Arcade Las Vegas

Start re:Invent week at full speed. Join Orca Security and Chainguard at F1 Arcade Las Vegas for an evening of great food, great company, and friendly competition. Race your peers head-to-head in immersive F1 simulators, whether you’re chasing the fastest lap or just along for the ride.

Spots are limited and reserved for security, cloud, and technology leaders. Register here

Date: Monday, November 30Time: 7:00 to 9:30 pm PTLocation: F1 Arcade Las Vegas, 3500 Las Vegas Blvd S

4. A night for the builders at The Sphere

Take a break from the re:Invent rush and trade notes with peers on how AI is changing who builds software, and how security keeps up. The evening starts with VIP entry to The Sphere’s Curve Bar for a private networking reception with passed hors d’oeuvres and a full bar. At 8:00 pm, we’ll head inside together for The Wizard of Oz on The Sphere’s wraparound screen.

This is an invitation-only evening for technology, cloud, and security leaders, and space is limited. Request your spot.

Date: Tuesday, December 1Time: 6:50 to 9:15 pm PT (arrive early to allow time for security screening)Location: The Sphere, 255 Sands Ave, Las Vegas

Can’t make it to Vegas?

You don’t need a badge to get started. Orca delivers security for the companies that build. As cloud, applications, AI, and app generation expand the attack surface, Orca turns risk into the context your teams need to act. You get complete visibility across cloud, AI, and application environments, risk correlated across every layer, and the exposures that matter most at the top of the list. Fix faster, and keep building with confidence.

Schedule a 1:1 demo with one of our experts.

articles.title: PHP2Shell: From the attacker’s perspective
articles.context: How far AI got us We tried to build the attack ourselves, with AI, working only from the published repair and our own test servers
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary:

Two faults in PHP, the software behind roughly seven out of ten websites, let a stranger on the internet run commands on a web server. A repair was published on 21 October.

We downloaded an attack tool that a stranger had published on GitHub and ran it, unchanged, against our own test server running an ordinary, unrepaired installation of PHP and it successfully took control.

We then built our own exploit with AI, starting from the published fix. Within hours, it ran commands on a standard PHP server – and worked against an ordinary WordPress site too.

What are CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619?

Why PHP vulnerabilities put most of the web at risk

When you open a web page, something has to build that page before it reaches you. For roughly seven out of ten websites, the software doing that job is PHP. It sits on the web server, assembles the page, and sends it to your browser. It is underneath WordPress, Drupal, Magento and a great many ordinary company websites.

What went wrong

CVE-2026-109618 leaves PHP’s internal state corrupted when its memory limit is reached, allowing attackers to hijack execution during cleanup. Its companion, CVE-2026-109619, causes a double free that exploit chains use to leak memory and defeat ASLR. Together, they can enable unauthenticated code execution and expose secrets; the fixes make allocation failures safe.

What we did

The question we wanted to answer was a practical one. How easy is it to create a working exploit with AI? And the answer is, it can get challenging. The guardrails of the modern models are strong and prevent the creation of a full-chain RCE exploit. But at the same time, they can always be bypassed. And none-the-less successful attack tools for this were still circulating within hours of the repair. The publishers are skilled hackers, and they were probably relying on local / non-guardrailed AI models.

How far AI got us

We tried to build the attack ourselves, with AI, working only from the published repair and our own test servers. AI found a way to make an ordinary web request use up all the memory PHP is allowed, on a server with entirely normal settings, before the website’s own code has even started. On the repaired version the same request is handled normally.

We then ran into tiring guardrails when attempting to ask for a full-chain RCE together with a memory leak primitive, and decided to switch to a different agent at this point. Once changed to another less restricted agent, it broke into a standard PHP server and ran commands in a matter of hours. Same attack then worked against an ordinary WordPress site.

successful exploit on 8.4.26

failed exploit on 8.4.27

Are AI-generated PHP exploits on GitHub a real threat?

The argument going round is that there are thousands of attack tools on GitHub, almost none of them work against a normal server, so the whole thing is overblown.

Most of those tools really are junk, written with AI by people with no way to tell whether they worked. Both things are true at once, though: the junk exists, and so do real attacks built with the same tools by people who check their results.

The speed is what to notice. When a similar flaw was found in another widely used program years ago, researchers were handed a full explanation of it and still took about three days to produce one working attack, against one specific version. Here nobody outside the disclosure knew what the flaw even was, and working attacks appeared within a day.

What made the difference was not a cleverer AI. It was the setup. That is the part to plan around. The flaw is still fiddly, and each version of PHP needs its own adjustments – but that is now a matter of leaving an AI to work through them, rather than a specialist’s week. The step from one broken server to several hundred has become a short one.

Why repairs help attackers too

A public fix also gives attackers a map of the flaw. PHP’s patch changed 300 files and included 127 regression tests designed to trigger the bugs – giving attackers expert-written examples to study. This is the same exact problem we’ve re-iterated with BGH. With vulnerable versions still available, anyone can compare behavior before and after the fix, just as we did. Publication starts the race: defenders must patch while attackers turn those clues into working exploits.

An unexpected finding

Working attacks existed before the flaw was public at all, with AI and nothing but the scraps already circulating. AI closed the gap between knowing a flaw exists and having a one-command tool, and that the internet then improved that tool for free. The window defenders assume they have, between a repair appearing and attacks following, can close before the repair is announced. This is a true game-changer in patch security.

How to protect PHP servers from CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619

Update PHP wherever you run it. We verified that the repair stops this attack. Versions 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12 and later contain it.

Find out where you run it. The harder half of the problem for most organisations is not patching, it is knowing which servers to patch. Old marketing sites, acquired brands, forgotten test machines and suppliers’ systems are where this will land.

If a server cannot be updated, take it off the public internet. Older versions of PHP have no repair available at all. For those, removing public access is the only real answer.

Assume that anything exposed and unpatched may already have been reached, and check it rather than hoping. Attempts against this were seen before the repair existed.

articles.title: PHP2Shell: What This Week Tells Us About the Web We Built
articles.context: com/blogs/security/amazon-threat-intelligence-identifies-php2shell-exploitation-prior-to-public-disclosure-in-madpot/ SecurityWeek: PHP2Shell patches land as first exploitation...
articles.full_text:
The week the web’s plumbing failed

On Wednesday afternoon, most of the world’s websites became exploitable at the same moment. The reason was PHP, the thirty-year-old language that still serves roughly seven out of ten sites you visit, including nearly every WordPress, Drupal, Magento and Joomla deployment on earth.

Two bugs, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, now known collectively as PHP2Shell, let an unauthenticated attacker run code on any server that handles PHP web requests. They are present in every PHP version back to 5.4, released in 2012. The coordinated disclosure broke down a day early, after leaks on 20 October. Exploit attempts hit honeypots before a patch existed. Government sites in Europe chose to go dark on patch day rather than stay online and exposed.

I have watched a great many “critical” bulletins come and go. Most of them deserve a calm Tuesday and a ticket in the queue. This one does not, and I want to explain why in business terms rather than technical ones. The technical story will be told well by the researchers who found it, and our own research team at Orca has published its analysis. The business story is the one your board, your CFO and your customers are going to ask you about.

What happened

The two flaws sit in the parts of PHP that every request touches: memory management and error handling. CVE-2026-109618 abuses how PHP bails out of an out-of-memory condition while request data is only half initialised. CVE-2026-109619 abuses global state that keeps pointing at request memory after that memory has been freed. Both are rated 9.2 on CVSS v4 and work without credentials, and both can also be used to read process memory, which is where your database passwords, API keys and session secrets happen to live.

What makes this different from the usual PHP advisory is the discovery story. The out-of-memory weakness was first noticed in 2020 and rediscovered during an audit in 2024. Nobody could prove it was exploitable, so it was never fixed. In August 2026, a small group of researchers, among them Calif and OpenAI, used frontier AI models to build the exploit chain that human researchers had judged impractical. The flaw did not change. The cost of proving it had.

Then the disclosure process came apart. A video with a working proof of concept was published by mistake. A container vendor shipped fixed images six hours before the coordinated release, giving anyone who cared to look a binary diff of the patch. The PHP Foundation pulled its release forward by a day. By the time the fixes landed, proof-of-concept exploits were already circulating and several vendors were watching attempts against their sensors.

When (UTC)

What happened

11 Aug 2026

The OOM-to-RCE chain is reported to the PHP security team by two independent parties; further attack vectors follow over the next weeks

17 Oct 2026

Amazon’s MadPot honeypots record an exploitation attempt, four days before public disclosure

20 Oct 2026

CVE IDs leak online; PHP issues a pre-announcement and moves the release up a day; a research team’s exploit video follows that evening

21 Oct, 02:00

First public proof-of-concept exploits appear; multiple actors begin probing honeypots

21 Oct, 03:02

Cloudflare deploys WAF rules for the known vectors, about eleven hours ahead of the patch

21 Oct, 07:41

Chainguard publishes patched container images, more than six hours before the embargo lifts

21 Oct, 14:00

PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 released; minimal source backports for 7.4 through 8.1; nothing for 5.4 through 7.3

21 Oct, afternoon

Government websites in Europe taken offline; exploitation reported “at scale” against the session upload-progress path

22 Oct 2026

Open-source scanners released; mass exploitation under way

The PHP team’s own position is blunt: there are no complete mitigations and updating is the only safe choice. Configuration tweaks can narrow specific attack paths. They do not close the hole.

Censys counts roughly 2.58 million internet-facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP. Every one of them that serves web requests, whether through PHP-FPM, mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP or LiteSpeed, is in scope.

Why this one hurts

The first thing to understand is that this is an engine bug, so every WordPress site, Drupal install and plugin inherits it. “Our application code is secure” is a true statement that does not matter. If your code runs on PHP, your code is the delivery vehicle for someone else’s payload.

The second thing is that almost nobody knows how much PHP they run. The flagship e-commerce platform, yes. The marketing microsite the agency built in 2019, the acquired brand’s storefront that was never migrated, the internal wiki, the staging box someone exposed to test a webhook, the customer portal your SaaS vendor runs on a hosting provider you have never heard of: these are the servers that will be compromised. Most of them are not in a CMDB. Many of them are not in anyone’s memory.

The third thing is what the attacker gets. The natural outcome of PHP2Shell is a web shell: a persistent backdoor living inside a legitimate, trusted, SSL-certified site that carries your brand. From there an attacker phishes your customers from your own domain, serves malware from a URL that every security product trusts, and reads credentials out of process memory to pivot into the cloud accounts behind the site. The breach does not look like a breach. It looks like your website.

The fourth thing is the patch itself. For PHP 8.2 and above there is a clean update. For 7.4 through 8.1 there are source backports, which means someone has to compile them. For anything older there is nothing at all. A great many enterprises are running end-of-life PHP underneath applications nobody wants to touch, because the last time someone touched them the site broke. Those organisations are now choosing between a planned outage and an unplanned compromise. That is where the stress in the market comes from this week: a bill for technical debt that was supposed to be deferred indefinitely has arrived all at once.

And the fifth thing is that the regulators are watching. Under NIS2, DORA and the SEC’s four-day disclosure rule, “we did not know we were running PHP” will be read as an admission.

Who

Exposure

What it costs

Companies with modern PHP (8.2+) and a known inventory

Patched within hours

A busy day and a hunt for anything that got in between 17 Oct and the patch

Companies with modern PHP and an unknown inventory

Patched the sites they know about

Weeks of discovery; the forgotten sites are the ones that get shelled

Companies on PHP 7.x or 8.0/8.1

Source backports only

Build and test effort, or an emergency upgrade with regression risk

Companies on PHP 5.x or 7.0 to 7.3

No fix exists

Take it offline, put it behind a WAF and hope, or rebuild

Everyone

Vendors and suppliers running PHP

Due diligence you cannot do yourself; you are only as patched as your weakest agency

The uncomfortable lessons

This embargo was handled by serious people with months of preparation, and it still leaked through a mistaken video upload and a vendor publishing early. Amazon saw exploitation attempts four days before anyone outside the circle was supposed to know. I would now treat any embargo as a courtesy. Plan on 24 to 48 hours of warning for the next one, and expect that warning to come from a honeypot rather than a mailing list.

The OOM flaw sat unfixed for six years because turning it into code execution looked impractical. Frontier models made it practical, so “not proven exploitable” should no longer be enough to close a ticket. The PHP Foundation has published 15 CVEs since July and says AI-assisted research is sending it far more reports than before. Every mature codebase written in C has a drawer full of bugs that were triaged as theoretical. That drawer is now being emptied, and not only by the people who will tell you about it.

Inventory was the control that mattered on Wednesday. Everyone was vulnerable, so the useful question was where PHP was running. The organisations that could answer that in minutes were patched within hours. The ones that could not are still discovering what they own, and they are discovering it in the same order the attackers are.

The sites that cannot be patched today were kept on old PHP because upgrading looked expensive and the risk looked abstract. For years that was a defensible trade-off. This week the risk became concrete, and the upgrade belongs on this quarter’s plan for anyone still running end-of-life runtimes on internet-facing systems.

The maintainers are carrying us. A handful of people at a foundation spent ten weeks fixing the engine that runs seventy percent of the web, under embargo, while watching that embargo fail around them. That arrangement held while bugs surfaced slowly. It will not hold once AI finds them faster than volunteers can fix them. Every enterprise that depends on PHP and does not fund the PHP Foundation is taking a free ride on infrastructure it would never accept for its own data centre.

What to do now

The next 72 hours are about containment. The next quarter is about never being in this position again.

In the next 72 hours

Find every PHP runtime you own, not every application you remember. Scan from the outside in. Include container images, serverless functions, appliances with embedded web interfaces, the marketing stack, acquired brands and anything an agency ever built for you. If you run Orca, the PHP2Shell news item in the platform includes a query that lists every asset with a PHP package installed across your connected cloud accounts.

Patch everything on 8.2 or later today, without waiting for a change window.

For 7.4 through 8.1, compile the backports or upgrade. For anything older, take it off the internet or put it behind a WAF with the PHP2Shell rules enabled, and accept that this is a bandage.

Assume compromise for any internet-facing PHP host that was unpatched after 17 October. In Orca, the PHP2Shell alerts flag which vulnerable hosts are reachable from the internet, so start there. Hunt for web shells, new admin users, modified core files and outbound connections you did not expect.

Rotate every secret that lived in PHP process memory on an exposed host: database credentials, API keys, cloud access keys, signing secrets.

Ask every vendor, agency and SaaS provider that touches your data the same question: which PHP version, patched when, and what did you find.

In the next quarter

Retire end-of-life PHP from anything internet-facing, with a budget line and an owner. If the application cannot move, treat the application itself as the risk.

Get secrets out of process memory. Short-lived credentials, workload identity and a secrets manager mean that the next memory-read bug leaks tokens that expire in an hour instead of keys that last for years.

Put an edge in front of everything. A CDN or WAF that can take a virtual patch in minutes bought the well-prepared organisations about eleven hours this week, which is often the difference between a hunt and a breach.

Create a pre-authorised emergency change path. The companies that patched within hours had already agreed, in calm times, who can push a change to production without a meeting.

Prioritise by exposure, not by CVSS. Two 9.2s on an internal admin tool behind a VPN are a Thursday. The same two on a public storefront holding card data are a board call. Your tooling should already know the difference.

How Orca can help

Most of the first 72 hours goes on finding out what you own, and that is where Orca starts. Orca’s agentless SideScanning reads installed packages directly from cloud workloads, so PHP is found on virtual machines, containers and container images without anything to deploy first. Detection for both CVEs went live in the platform on 21 October.

Finding PHP answers half of the question. The other half is deciding what to patch first and what an attacker could reach from each host. Each PHP2Shell alert shows whether the asset is reachable from the internet, whether the vulnerable component is loaded at runtime, and how critical it is to the business.

For the hunt and the clean-up, Orca’s lightweight eBPF Sensor adds runtime visibility on the hosts where it is deployed, and the asset graph shows which keys and cloud roles each exposed host holds, and that is where secret rotation should start.

Several customers told us the Early Intel query in the platform’s From the News item gave them a head start, letting them find their PHP hosts and begin mitigating before the official advisory went out.

None of this replaces patching. It shortens the time between the advisory and knowing where to patch first.

What this means for the next two years

PHP2Shell is the first widely visible instance of a pattern that will define vulnerability management for the rest of this decade.

AI has collapsed the cost of turning a theoretical bug into a working exploit. The backlog of “unproven” memory-safety issues in the foundational C codebases of the internet, the interpreters, the TLS libraries, the image parsers, the web servers, is enormous, and it was accumulated in an era when proving exploitability took a specialist a month. That era ended this summer. Expect the same story, with different names, in Python, Ruby, Node, OpenSSL and the kernel. Expect it more than once a quarter. Every CISO should assume their foundational dependencies have critical bugs. What they can still influence is whether they hear about them through a coordinated advisory or through an incident.

The window between disclosure and mass exploitation is now measured in hours, and sometimes it is negative. Monthly patch cycles were designed for a world where attackers needed weeks to weaponise a bug. For anything that faces the internet, that cadence is obsolete. The operating model that survives this decade treats patching exposed systems as a continuous process with a pre-approved fast lane, and treats a virtual patch at the edge as the normal first response rather than an exotic one. It also depends on an inventory that can answer “where do we run X” in a minute, across cloud, on-premises, containers, vendors and the long tail of forgotten sites.

If there is a single takeaway, it is about time. The weakness had been in PHP since 2012, the working exploit was about two months old, and the response had to happen within hours. The organisations under the most stress this week are the ones whose decision-making was built for a slower world, whatever the quality of their security teams. Most of what fixes that is deciding things in advance, so that the answers already exist before the next disclosure.

Sources

Calif: PHP2Shell writeup, https://calif.io/php2shell/

Amazon Threat Intelligence: PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure, https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/amazon-threat-intelligence-identifies-php2shell-exploitation-prior-to-public-disclosure-in-madpot/

SecurityWeek: PHP2Shell patches land as first exploitation attempts hit sensors, https://www.securityweek.com/php2shell-patches-land-as-first-exploitation-attempts-hit-sensors/

Krebs on Security: Widespread PHP flaw may cause many site outages, https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/10/widespread-php-flaw-may-cause-many-site-outages-today/

articles.title: Benchmark Your AI Security Maturity in Under a Minute
articles.context: In the 2026 State of AI Security report, the Orca Research Pod found that 51
articles.full_text:
Five years ago, AI security was a forward-looking line item. Today it’s an operational reality, and the data shows most security programs haven’t caught up.

In the 2026 State of AI Security report, the Orca Research Pod found that 51.5% of organizations are building custom AI apps. 56% are running agent frameworks in production. This isn’t a pilot phase anymore. Agents have real cloud permissions. RAG pipelines are wired into sensitive data. Models are fine-tuned on proprietary datasets. It’s production infrastructure now, and nobody’s wrapped the usual production controls around any of it.

The gap is everywhere in the report:

81% of organizations with AI packages carry at least one known vulnerability, up from 62% two years ago. Half of those alerts have public exploits.

57.1% of Bedrock-using organizations run agents with no safety guardrails configured.

Between 87% and 98% of AI workloads across AWS, Azure, and GCP have never had customer-managed encryption turned on.

33% of organizations have GitHub Copilot deployed, and Stanford research found developers using AI coding assistants write measurably less secure code while rating it as more secure than it is.

This isn’t one misconfiguration. It’s AI shipping faster than the governance meant to secure it, and that now includes the applications AI itself is generating.

Regulation is closing that gap on its own timeline. The EU AI Act’s high-risk obligations take effect August 2, 2026, with fines up to €35M or 7% of global turnover. Colorado’s amended AI law takes effect January 1, 2027. If you deploy AI in the EU or in high-risk use cases like hiring, credit, or healthcare, the misconfigurations in this report are compliance liabilities today.

Your organization has AI risk. The adoption numbers guarantee it. What matters is whether you can show where you stand, to a regulator, a board, or your own team, before someone else asks first.

Benchmark Where You Actually Stand, Then Get Your Next Step

Industry-wide numbers tell you what the space looks like. Where your organization falls against them tells you what to do Monday morning.

Orca’s AI Security Readiness Assessment gives you that read in five questions and under a minute. No email required to see your score. It covers the five domains where AI risk lands first for security leaders:

AI visibility — sanctioned and shadow AI across your cloud and SaaS footprint. The layer most CISOs say they can’t fully see.

Data exposure — what sensitive data can reach generative AI tools, and whether anyone has mapped that path

AI in your SOC — whether AI is doing real security work for your team, or just adding another surface to defend

AI AppGen security — whether the apps and code your AI tools are generating get the same scrutiny as the code your developers write by hand

Governance — what you could put in front of a regulator today, not what your policy says you’d eventually produce

Wherever you land, your result comes with a next step matched to it, not a generic thank-you page. Depending on where your organization scores, that might be early access to research, a look at how peers are approaching AI security, or a curated set of resources built to close the gaps your assessment surfaces.

Five questions. Under a minute. What you do with the answer is the part that matters.

articles.title: From Security Debt to Zero Criticals: Orca MCP and Claude Code
articles.context: To catch risky code before it reaches production, the team flipped Orca’s PR scanning from warn to block for criticals with a fix available, so a new one can’t land on the main...
articles.full_text:
Security debt behaves like the financial kind. Nobody takes it on deliberately. It accrues one skipped base image bump at a time, and the interest shows up as a backlog no one owns.

The pattern is familiar to anyone who has inherited a cloud estate. Hundreds of repos. A fleet of containers nobody fully owns. A vulnerability backlog that earlier cleanup efforts never finished, because every time security handed engineering a list, engineering asked the same question: which of these actually matter?

Then leadership sets a date. Every critical fixed by the end of the month. The security team that has to deliver is small, and the engineers who can fix things live in their own tools. Increasingly that tool is a coding agent that is already reading the repo and writing the diff. The last place they want to be is a security console, and nobody has patience for automation that creates work instead of removing it.

Most tools promise a queue of tickets or auto-generated fix PRs waiting each morning. But can any tool hand the agent enough truth, and enough context, that an engineer would look at what came back and have the confidence to merge it? Here’s how one of our customers did it with Orca.

Why coding agents can’t fix vulnerabilities safely on their own

Give a coding agent a CVE ID and a repo and it will produce a plausible diff, but two things are missing.

The first is ground truth. Which of the thousand findings is real, reachable, and running in production? Where does the vulnerable package actually live: pinned in a requirements.txt or package.json, installed by a RUN apt-get line in a Dockerfile, or inherited from a base image in the FROM line that nobody on the team builds? And which repo, out of hundreds, produced the container that is actually running? The agent can grep for a package name, but grepping across hundreds of repos is how you patch the wrong service.

The second is guardrails. Left alone, an agent will happily bump a major version, swap a base image distro, or push to main because that resolved the finding fastest. Any one of those closes the alert but breaks the service.

Both gaps come down to context and guardrails, and both are solvable today. The stack that solves them has three parts:

Orca supplies the context

Orca MCP Server delivers it to the coding agent

A guided skill sets the guardrails

What context Orca gives the coding agent

A coding agent can read a repo. It cannot see what is running, what is exposed, or which image a container came from. That is what Orca contributes, and three pieces of it carry the fix.

Code origin. Orca can trace dev risk to production by mapping a running workload back to the code that produced it: the Dockerfile that built the image, the Terraform that deployed the service, the Helm chart that configured it. Any one of those is enough to land the agent in the right repo. For a vulnerability, that is the difference between “there is a vulnerable OpenSSL somewhere in production” and “this Dockerfile, in this repo, line 3.”

Package and image context. The alert carries the installed version, the fixed versions, and whether the issue is an OS package or an application dependency. That lets the skill pick the smallest patched version in the track already installed instead of guessing at a release that happens to be newer.

Risk context. Exposure, attack path analysis, and whether the asset holds sensitive data. The agent doesn’t need this to write the fix. The engineer needs it to understand why this one is first, and the skill carries it into the PR description so the reviewer isn’t rebuilding the case from scratch.

Without those three, the agent produces a diff. With them, it produces a diff an engineer can defend: the right repo, the right line, the smallest version that closes the finding, and the reason it was worth doing today.

How the remediation skill works in Claude Code, step by step

The engineer opens Claude Code with the Orca MCP connected and hands the skill an alert ID. From there it runs a fixed playbook.

Screenshot of giving Claude an alert ID from Orca.

Context gathering: Claude pulls the alert through the MCP, then the code origin. It confirms the repo, the file, and the exact line before touching anything.

Decision: The skill checks the finding against a short list of issue types it is allowed to fix. For those, it picks the smallest version bump that closes the finding and keeps base images on the same distro. Anything outside that list, including major-version upgrades, end-of-life base images, or a repo that has changed since the scan, stops the run with an explanation instead of a guess.

Generation: Claude clones the repo, edits the line, and validates the change. When Docker is available locally, the agent builds the image to confirm the fix before it hands anything back.

Review: The output is a diff. The skill never commits, never pushes, and never touches cloud state. The engineer reads it and approves. Only then does it open a PR on a new branch and write a comment and an in-progress status back to the Orca alert. Once the fix is merged and deployed, Orca closes the alert automatically on the next scan.

Screenshot of the output from the skill – a diff.

Why engineers trusted AI-generated fixes

That last rule did more for adoption than anything else. Engineers trusted the output because it could not do anything they hadn’t read first. The skill was written in the open agent skills format, so the same file runs in Cursor, Codex, or whatever else a team has standardized on. Like most orgs, our customer hadn’t settled on a single coding agent. A remediation workflow that works regardless of which one an engineer opens was a hard requirement.

Results: zero critical vulnerabilities in 30 days

By the deadline, our customer had zero critical alerts. Along the way the same skill cleared more than 200 alerts in a month, every fix produced by Claude Code with Orca’s data behind it and every one merged by an engineer who had read the diff. Security and engineering worked the backlog together, and the security lead was in Claude Code running the skill alongside them.

Orca’s vulnerability management handled the security reasoning: which findings were real and exposed, and where the code that produced them lived. The coding agent did the software engineering. The handoff between the two teams, the step that used to stall every cleanup effort, shrank to a code review.

Keeping the security debt from landing

The same skill now runs on a schedule against new software composition analysis (SCA) alerts and opens a PR for each one before anyone has to ask. To catch risky code before it reaches production, the team flipped Orca’s PR scanning from warn to block for criticals with a fix available, so a new one can’t land on the main branch without the fix in hand.

It also changed how they ship. Once engineering saw that a service with its build definition in a repo got a reviewable fix in minutes, that became the deployment standard. Security influenced an engineering practice without writing a policy because the faster path and the more secure path were the same path.

Screenshot of Orca’s scan results in a pull request.

Orca already knows what is running, what is exposed, and where the code lives. The MCP Server already puts that in front of the coding agent your engineers use every day. A skill turns the two into a workflow with guardrails.

Security debt doesn’t have to keep compounding. This team paid theirs down to zero criticals in a month, and the guardrails they set have prevented new debt from landing.

Get started with the Orca MCP Server

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard introduced by Anthropic that lets AI assistants connect to external data sources. The Orca MCP Server brings your Orca environment into Claude, making cloud security intelligence accessible through natural language and rich, structured output.

The Orca MCP Server also brings AI-powered investigation and remediation into the tools your engineers already use. For more ways to use it, see: AI chat prompts for the Orca MCP Server.

articles.title: How to Build Your Actual Network Map with Custom Agents in Orca
articles.context: Neither describes what an attacker on the internet can actually reach today
articles.full_text:
Ask most teams for a map of their network and you’ll get one of two things: a diagram someone drew for an audit two years ago, or an export from the firewall and cloud consoles showing what each rule allows. Both describe intent. Neither describes what an attacker on the internet can actually reach today.

The gap between the two is where incidents start. A database is marked “public network access enabled” but sits behind a private endpoint, so it isn’t reachable at all. A load balancer looks locked down in one console, but a CDN in front of it forwards traffic from anywhere. A subdomain still points at a cloud resource that was deleted months ago, and anyone can claim it.

Orca approaches the network map from the attacker’s side: follow the full path to every asset, then test the perimeter from the outside. Custom Agents turn that data into a map you can keep current without redrawing it by hand.

What usually goes into a network map?

A useful network map answers a short list of questions. Traditionally, each answer comes from a different source, maintained by a different team:

What the map needs

Where it usually comes from

What Orca adds

An inventory of assets and addresses

CMDB, IP address management, spreadsheets

Cloud asset inventory across accounts, plus discovered domains, subdomains, and IP addresses

The ways in from the internet

Security group and load balancer configurations

An exposure rating for every asset, calculated across the full network path

The controls in front of each asset

Firewall, security group, and WAF rule exports

Security groups, cloud firewalls, Check Point firewalls, WAFs, and CDNs evaluated together, with labels showing which assets are fully or partly behind a WAF

Open ports and running services

Port scans, configuration review

Exposure rated per port, for services Orca finds running on the asset

Application and API endpoints

API gateway configurations, developer documentation

Discovered API endpoints, Swagger views, and a Network Exposure graph linking open ports to the application endpoints behind them

The condition of the perimeter

An annual penetration test

Ongoing external probing for subdomain takeover risk, certificate problems, exposed files, and debug panels

What sits behind the perimeter

Team knowledge

Attack paths, crown jewels, and the Internet and IAM Exposure Graph

The traditional column has a common weakness: each source describes one layer, in one tool, as configured. Combining them is often done manually and made obsolete quickly.

Why isn’t the configuration enough?

Every cloud provider exposes its own public access settings, such as Azure’s PublicNetworkAccess flag. That setting records what a resource permits. It doesn’t answer whether the resource can be reached from the internet, and the two answers are often different.

Orca calculates exposure by following the full network path to each resource: firewall rules, network security groups, private endpoints, load balancers, WAFs, and CDNs. A resource that permits public access but sits behind a private endpoint isn’t reachable, so Orca doesn’t classify it as Public Facing. A virtual machine with a strict security group that receives traffic forwarded by a load balancer inherits the load balancer’s exposure.

Each asset ends up with one of a small set of exposure ratings:

Public Facing: open to all IPv4 addresses

Internet Facing: reachable from specific external addresses, including through CDNs

Trusted Access: reachable only from IP ranges you’ve defined as trusted

None: no external exposure found

Orca also rates exposure per port. An asset can be Internet Facing on port 443 while its other three open ports are Trusted Access or None. That’s the difference between “this server is exposed” and “this one service on this server is exposed,” and it’s the level of detail a network map needs.

A firewall rule tells you what one control allows. A network map has to show what the aggregation of controls allows, port by port.

What does testing from the outside add?

Network path analysis tells you what should be reachable. Orca’s external scanning and API security testing check what the perimeter looks like from the internet.

Orca probes the domains, subdomains, and endpoints it discovers and checks them against its Web & API Exposure Posture framework:

Domain and takeover risks: expiring or expired domains, subdomains and CloudFront distributions at risk of takeover

TLS and certificate hygiene: deprecated SSL or TLS versions, expired, self-signed, or mismatched certificates, unencrypted pages with password fields

Exposed files and artifacts: environment variable files, .git paths, swagger.json files, phpinfo pages, and exposed secrets

Debug and admin panels: known tools running in debug mode or exposing sensitive data without authentication

Reputation: hosts and IP addresses that rate badly with reputation engines

These are findings no firewall export will show you, because they live in DNS records, web servers, and application code rather than in network rules.

For the addresses that matter most, the Attack Surface Red Agent goes further. It runs safe, AI-driven testing against a single domain or IP address, finding new endpoints and web vulnerabilities, and produces a structured report of what it scanned and what it found.

How does a Custom Agent turn this into a map?

The data above already lives in Orca. A Custom Agent assembles it into a map, organized the way your teams work, and keeps it current.

Context: Global Context

Trigger: Schedule, weekly

Tools: Send Custom Slack Message, Open Jira Cloud Custom Ticket

Use previous run as context: On

## Configuration target subscription = [enter subscription name in quotes] depth (topology or full) = [enter topology or full] max resources shown per subnet = [enter a number] security overlay = [on/off] roll up empty VNets = [on/off] ## Role You are a cloud network architect mapping one Azure subscription from Orca’s inventory for a security engineer who has never seen it. Report only what the inventory contains. An honest, incomplete map is better than a confident guess. ## Ground rules * Evidence: Every placement, edge, and finding must trace to a field you actually read that held a value. If you don’t know, say “unknown” and list the candidates. * Nulls: Never call a field empty unless you inspected it. If it’s empty where it shouldn’t be, re-fetch once and flag the disagreement. ## Process 1. Retrieve: Pull VNets, subnets, NICs, NSGs, VMs (including scale-set instances), AKS clusters, load balancers, bastions, NAT gateways, route tables, and private endpoints. Full runs also pull PaaS services and public IPs. Keep a ledger of records retrieved vs. total. Any shortfall makes the run INCOMPLETE, and that goes in the first sentence. 2. Frame: Attach subnets to VNets by parsing the SubnetId path. 3. Place workloads: * Match region + CIDR first, never CIDR alone. * Use NIC traversal only to resolve ambiguity. * Use naming or resource-group convention as a last resort, clearly marked. * Label each asset Confirmed, Inferred, Convention, Ambiguous, or Unplaceable. 4. Edges: Draw subnet → NAT/route table/bastion, NIC → public IP, load balancer → backends, and private endpoint → PaaS. Never infer peering. 5. Security overlay:Use Orca’s computed exposure, crown-jewel, and risk fields instead of re-reading NSG rules. Flag internet-facing crown jewels first, then lateral-movement and segmentation issues. Name the exact open port. ## Output * summary * retrieval ledger * text hierarchy * subnet inventory table * findings and gaps ### Example Text Hierarchy: Example 10.5.0.0/16 centralus RG:orca-demo ├── default 10.5.0.0/24 [NSG: NIC-level only] │ ├── ~ orca-ubuntu-prod 10.5.0.8 pub:52.230.192.27 SSH:22 CJ OrcaScore:9.7 internet-facing │ ├── ~ orca-web-server 10.5.0.4 pub:20.9.73.217 SSH:22 CJ OrcaScore:8.9 internet-facing ├── myappgatewaysubnet 10.5.2.0/24 │ └── NOT MODELLED: Application Gateway (absent from Orca) └── AzureBastionSubnet 10.5.1.0/26 └── EMPTY (test-vm-vnet-bastion is in csd-4100, not this VNet) ## Self-checks zero orphan subnets · every VM has a private IP · no model unexpectedly returns zero · placement counts add up

See the delta between each run in the Agent Feed.

Since we instructed the agent to build a text hierarchy of the topology, we can see an example of this in the latest result of the Agent Feed for the Network Map Custom Agent.

Example text hierarchy from the Network Map Custom Agent in Orca.

Lastly, as part of the output, we wanted to see the security findings and gaps,

Why does the weekly comparison matter?

A network map is only useful while it’s accurate. Cloud environments change daily, so a static diagram is out of date as soon as it’s finished.

Because the agent can read its previous run, each report shows changes rather than a full restatement: a new internet-facing port, a load balancer that lost its WAF, a subdomain that became a takeover candidate, a new attack path to a crown jewel. That’s the part of the map your team needs to act on, and the part that’s hardest to see by comparing two exports by eye.

When the map flags a new or high-risk address, run the Attack Surface Red Agent against it for a deeper test.
